key_insight: Ly and Gong propose that deep learning’s unpredictability arises from fractal basin geometry: starting points that lead to different outcomes are interwoven at extremely fine scales. Greater precision may therefore offer little improvement in predicting the final result.
problem_solved: The paper addresses why deep learning outcomes can remain difficult to predict and reproduce, even when differences in starting conditions are very small.
method: Frame training outcomes in terms of basins: sets of starting points that lead to the same outcome.
Propose that these basins have fractal geometry, with different outcomes interwoven at arbitrarily fine scales.
Connect this geometry to limits on how much increased precision can improve predictability and reproducibility.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, the proposed mechanism suggests that tighter numerical precision alone may not guarantee reproducible training. It motivates evaluating variability across runs rather than relying on a single outcome.
visual_elements: Color-coded basin map showing nearby starting points leading to different outcomes.
Nested zoom panels illustrating interwoven outcome regions at progressively finer scales.
Two nearly identical starting points with training paths ending in different outcomes.
Conceptual chart showing diminishing prediction gains as starting-point precision increases.
paper_title: Fractal basin geometry and the limits to predictability and reproducibility in deep learning
